items.title: Nvidia’s Q3 earnings hit the mark, without mentioning the whole Jensen Huang thing
items.summary: Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company's Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure, or possible attempt at a return. On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked t
items.content:
Nvidia’s Q3 revenue has more than doubled, with income from data centers up 110 percent from last year, to $107.6 billion.

Interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress announced the company’s Q3 earnings on Tuesday, without initially mentioning former CEO Jensen Huang or the details of his departure , or possible attempt at a return . On the earnings call accompanying the release, board chair Harvey Jones kicked things off by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO,” and that “we will not be addressing or taking questions on today’s call regarding the circumstances of Jensen’s resignation and the ongoing investigation,” before Kress started with her comments on the results.

As it predicted in the last financial update , Nvidia is now on the list of companies that have pulled in over $100 billion in a single quarter, with revenues of $115.8 billion, up 103 percent from the same period last year and higher than its expectation of $108 billion. This quarter’s figures include data center revenues of $107.6 billion, which were up 110 percent, and edge computing (which includes the consumer gaming PC business and devices like the new RTX Spark laptops ) revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42 percent.

The company reported $65.3 billion in profit, a new record.

In the fourth quarter, Nvidia expects revenues of $130 billion.

items.title: Nike’s new air sole technology can mix soft and firm cushioning
items.summary: In 2024, Nike announced its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The company is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using
items.content:
The first shoes with Nike’s new Tuned Air technology will be available for runners starting in late 2027.﻿

In 2024, Nike announced its Air Max 1000 that were manufactured using a 3D-printing process resulting in a shoe that had a uniform silhouette but varying areas of support and flexibility throughout. The company is now doing something similar with its iconic air-filled soles using its new Tuned Air technology . While previously the level of cushioning in Nike Air shoes was uniform across the entire sole, a new manufacturing process can produce multiple air pockets with varying levels of cushioning and stability.

Nike has been putting air pockets into its shoes for nearly 50 years as a way to increase comfort and cushioning while making them lighter. Its air pockets have even found their way into apparel as a way to improve insulation by trapping body heat, but Nike plans to use its new Tuned Air technology as a way to customize the cushioning experience in its shoes and tailor them to specific athletes and sports. The first shoes featuring the technology are expected to arrive in late 2027 and will be targeted at runners.

While one of Nike’s earliest successes was track shoes with a grip design inspired by a waffle iron , the company credits the “vibrant colors on magazine covers” as the inspiration for its latest shoe technology. A Tuned Air sole is manufactured using a “proprietary digital print and selective lamination process” where an ink is applied in specific patterns that define where the layers bond to each other. This process can be used to create internal pockets in an unlimited combination of shapes and sizes, and by fine-tuning how much air is in each of those pockets, some parts of the sole can feel firmer while others feel softer.

The Tuned Air technology will not only allow Nike to highly customize the fit and feel of air sole shoes for different sports, it will also help keep the benefits of the custom tuning consistent across different sizes. The new manufacturing process will also help reduce the amount of time it takes Nike to go from a concept for a new shoe to a final design ready for production. “Prototypes that once took three weeks can now be made in three days,” the company claims in a release today. That gives Nike’s designers more time to refine new shoes, and more opportunity to experiment.

items.title: Google joins the tech outage trend by announcing it’s not having one
items.summary: With tech outages seemingly everywhere, Google took the unusual step of announcing that Gmail is working just fine, actually.
items.content:
Was Google feeling a little left out of the recent wave of tech outages? The company took to X on Tuesday to announce that its Gmail service is actually running just fine. In a post, the company said it was not currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption and reminded users they could always check Gmail’s real-time status on its online dashboard .

As it turns out, the company was trying to head off reports of a Gmail outage that began circulating on X on Tuesday around the same time that Apple was seeing a number of verified outages of its own . While some posts on the social network suggested Gmail was experiencing a disruption, others said they were not having any problems.

The concerns seemed to stem from an X post by Downdetector, a crowdsourced website where users can report service disruptions themselves and see if others are having problems. Downdetector is not an official source for verifying or understanding the true scope of internet outages, and as people become more concerned about possible cyberattacks, the site’s data may become less valuable over time if every minor glitch and hiccup is reported as an “outage” by non-technical users.

The fact that Google had to announce it was not having an outage speaks to the growing anxiety around the reliability of major tech services. Over the past week, Apple and Microsoft experienced outages, an FAA network failure led to a nationwide ground stop, and some banks and airlines also reported disruptions.

However, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox Business Network’s “The Claman Countdown” on Tuesday that the U.S. is not currently facing coordinated cyberattacks. He told the outlet, “We do not see the indicia of a coordinated cyberattack — let me just be clear about that — and we do not see the indicia of state-sponsored activity here.”

Instead, Clayton attributed the rise in issues to businesses patching their systems. The patching may be a downstream effect of AI, as newer models have become increasingly adept at uncovering previously unknown vulnerabilities. “They’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place,” he said, adding that this is happening at “a much larger scale” than before.

As a result, some of the systems are “not coming back as expected in all cases,” he added.

items.title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
items.summary: Article URL: https://calif.io/java4shell/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50538240 Points: 569 # Comments: 149
items.content:
Write once, RCE everywhere

Story by the New York Times

A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution.

Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘

After we disclosed PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.

Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL).

While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language , powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems.

Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single = :

In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by = .

Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs.

The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own.

Here are a demo video of the exploits running:

Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software.

But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life.

To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted.

As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker , part human, part AI.

It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200.

One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI.

Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it.

Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk.

Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place?

If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not.

Earlier this year we found Squidbleed , an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed.

Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains.

This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

items.title: Not even Sam Altman is safe from AI deepfakes on Instagram
items.summary: Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content - including, as of late, from one of Meta's most prominent executives. Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company's consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated
items.content:
Meta’s chief AI officer posted an AI video of a top competitor. It’s allowed under Meta’s AI policy.﻿

Instagram is filled with people posting deepfaked content — including, as of late, from one of Meta’s most prominent executives.

Earlier in November, Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, shared a short clip to promote Muse, the company’s consumer AI agent. In the AI-generated clip, Wang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and Jolly, the anthropomorphic mascot of Muse, are on a four-way video call. When Altman joins the call he’s dressed like Jolly, wearing a furry hooded suit and face paint to look like the cutesy character. The clip is captioned “When the homies meet about openai product strategy,” a reference to the AI agent race and the recent popularity of Muse.

Just a few years ago, AI content portraying real people led to strong public statements rebuking the use of the technology to imitate humans. In some cases legal action was threatened . Now, AI content has become part of the texture of a new reality, especially on social media. Leading up to the midterm elections, for example, political groups ran millions of dollars’ worth of AI-generated ads attacking opponents.

Wang has been doing a lot of what some have described as “anti-PR” to promote Muse, tweeting hundreds of times and referring to more traditional marketers as “corposlops.” Still, a major tech executive posting an AI video of a competitor is notable, especially on a platform that’s been criticized recently over AI-generated content. After an AI-generated image of actress Mia Goth gained traction in October, the Pearl star’s representative told The Verge it was “incomprehensible” that Instagram allowed the image to spread instead of focusing on the “protection and integrity of a public figure’s likeness.” Other celebrities, including Scarlett Johansson, are regularly the subject of sexualized AI imagery; Meta has removed some accounts in the past that it found to be posing as someone else and using their likeness.

Meta requires AI-generated videos depicting people to be labeled as AI, like Wang’s post is. Static images, however, have no such requirement, meaning the AI image of Goth had no disclosure. To make matters worse, the image was shared by a fan account with a blue verification badge given by Instagram.

Reached for comment, Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton noted that Wang’s post is labeled as AI content. Clayton also pointed out that Altman has made his likeness available for AI content generation, as when OpenAI launched its Sora app (and it was quickly flooded with fake Altman videos). OpenAI didn’t respond to requests for comment.

items.content:
젠슨 황 전 엔비디아 CEO가 퇴진 이후 처음으로 공식 성명을 내고 이사회가 원한다면 CEO로 복귀하겠다는 뜻을 밝혔다. 직원과 투자자, 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들에 이어 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령까지 복귀를 지지하고 있지만, 엔비디아 이사회는 복귀를 검토하지 않는 것으로 알려졌다.

황 전 CEO는 17일(현지시간) 성명을 통해 복귀 의사를 공개적으로 밝혔다. 지난 12일 사임한 이후 첫 공식 입장이다.

그는 "사임 이후 엔비디아 직원과 투자자, 사업 파트너, 고객들로부터 CEO로 복귀해 달라는 요청이 쏟아졌다"라며 "이사회가 내 복귀가 주주와 직원, 회사와 미국에 최선이라고 판단한다면 기꺼이 CEO로 돌아가겠다"라고 말했다.

또 "이사회에 문제를 일으킨 데 대해 깊이 유감스럽게 생각한다"라며 "내 잘못을 전적으로 인정하고 이사회의 독립적인 조사에 적극적으로 협조하겠다"라고 밝혔다.

그가 공개적으로 복귀 의사를 밝힌 것은 이번이 처음이다. 앞서 직원과 주주, 일론 머스크 CEO 등 실리콘밸리 주요 인사들이 복귀를 요구했으며, 트럼프 대통령도 이를 지지했다.

그러나 엔비디아 이사회는 복귀를 논의하지 않고 있다. 로이터는 16일 정통한 소식통 3명을 인용해 이사회가 복귀를 검토하지 않는다고 보도했다. 황 전 CEO의 이번 성명에 대한 논평 요청에도 응답하지 않았다.

엔비디아는 이날 국가 안보와 수출 통제 준수 여부를 감독하는 이사회 산하 상설위원회도 신설했다. 수잔 노라 존슨 이사가 위원장을 맡으며, 미국의 국가 안보 정책과 수출 규정 준수, 글로벌 무역 위험을 직접 감독한다. 황 전 CEO 퇴진 이후 첫 번째 주요 지배구조 개편이다.

그의 복귀 문제는 분기 실적 발표를 앞두고 주목받고 있다. 엔비디아는 17일 미국 증시 마감 후 실적을 발표할 예정이며, 콜레트 크레스 임시 CEO가 투자자들에게 향후 사업 전망을 설명하게 된다.

그러나 복귀하더라도 엔비디아의 경영 문제가 모두 해결되는 것은 아니라는 지적도 나온다.

엔비디아 주가는 사생활 논란이 불거지기 전부터 AI 데이터센터 투자 둔화 가능성과 막대한 부채를 동원한 AI 인프라 투자에 대한 의문으로 하락하고 있었다. 지난 10월 최고치 이후 시가총액이 약 2조달러(약 2670조원) 감소했으며, 세계 시가총액 1위 자리도 애플과 MS에 내줬다.

벤 프레스턴 오르비스 글로벌 주식 전략 담당자는 그의 복귀가 회사의 문제를 반드시 해결해 주지는 못할 것이라고 평가했다. 특히 엔비디아가 고객사에 투자하거나 자금을 지원해 AI 칩 판매를 뒷받침해 온 사업 구조가 규제 당국의 조사 대상이 될 가능성도 제기했다.

미국 정부와 의회의 수출 통제 관련 조사도 계속되고 있다. 앨리스 황이 주요 주주로 있던 싱가포르 클라우드 기업 메가스피드는 중국으로의 AI 칩 우회 공급 의혹으로 조사를 받고 있으며, 관련 혐의를 부인하고 있다. 미국 정보기관도 앨리스 황과 중국 정보기관의 관계를 조사 중인 것으로 알려졌다.

이제 관심은 이사회의 판단에 모이고 있다. 엔비디아가 독립 조사와 수출 통제 감독 체계 개편을 진행하는 가운데, AI 투자 수익성에 대한 시장의 의문도 계속되고 있어 황 전 CEO의 복귀만으로 경영 불확실성을 해소하기는 어려운 상황이다.

items.title: “Trump was in bed with Jensen”: Critics balk at Huang’s wish to return to Nvidia
items.summary: “I love our country”: Jensen Huang’s apology comes amid escalating Nvidia probes.
items.content:
On Monday, large trucks began circling the streets of Washington, DC, carrying billboards urging Congress to investigate the Trump administration’s ties with Nvidia’s disgraced CEO Jensen Huang.

“Jensen was in bed with a spy from China,” the billboards created by the Tech Oversight Project (TOP) alleged. “Trump was in bed with Jensen.” TOP is a nonprofit that describes itself as “dedicated to reining in Big Tech.”

Currently, Trump is supporting a campaign to bring back Huang as Nvidia’s CEO—despite many Republicans calling it a “ horrible idea. ” Breaking his silence, Huang issued a statement Tuesday saying he would be “honored” to return, but the board said reinstatement is not under consideration as an internal investigation into US spying claims remains ongoing. Huang used the moment to say that his interests align with the US’s, saying:

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. Nvidia has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like Nvidia be possible. I love our country, and I love Nvidia.

Trump may have learned as early as this spring that Huang was potentially the target of Chinese espionage, but the president claimed recently that he didn’t know Huang was potentially exposed to a Chinese spy as he was becoming a prominent part of Trump’s inner circle, CNN reported .

If Trump wasn’t adequately briefed, it raises question about whether the White House acted with “sufficient urgency” to address a serious espionage threat, CNN said. But if Trump is deflecting, an even “graver question” will emerge about why Trump didn’t act on information and instead continued to keep Huang close, CNN said.

Instead of distancing himself from the Nvidia CEO, Trump invited Huang to sit at the head table during a state dinner with China’s president Xi Jinping, and last month, Trump awarded Huang the National Medal of Science, the nation’s highest scientiﬁc honor, for his AI achievements.

“Not only has he continued to do nothing, he’s invited that very CEO into the White House and on state visits to China with him,” Sacha Haworth, TOP’s founder and CEO, told Ars. “And the question we all have to ask is ‘why on Earth would he do that?’”

What Trump and Nvidia knew—and when—have become central questions for some Republicans, as well as top Democrats who plan to investigate the scandal when they assume control of key committees in Congress next year. Andrew Yoon, head of research for a nonprofit called CivAI, which warns the public of dangers from AI, told Ars that Huang doesn’t need to be compromised by China to have endangered the US. Prioritizing boosting profits over national security alone is “pretty concerning.”

“I think the most notable thing here is that Jensen Huang has been at the absolute forefront of lobbying to be able to sell chips to China,” Yoon said. “He has leveraged his very deep relationships with government, especially President Trump, in order to be able to sell as many Nvidia chips to China as he can get away with. If he could be selling Blackwell chips to China, I’m sure he would be.”

Yoon noted that evidence suggests some Chinese AI models have been trained on Blackwell chips. Even with China’s push to prioritize domestic chipmakers like Huawei, Nvidia chips remain “indispensable” to China’s frontier AI goals, Yoon said. And national security experts fear that access to high-end chips will help China advance its military AI or gain economic ground.

The White House isn’t commenting on Trump’s relationship with Huang. Among the lawmakers accusing the Trump administration of “corruption” is Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D–Conn.), The Wall Street Journal reported . He has already asked the White House to “preserve all communications” between Trump and Huang.

Other lawmakers are “seeking more information about what Trump knew about the relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang,” the former Megaspeed CEO whom Huang admitted to having an affair with. They also want to know more about “the administration’s failure to stop artiﬁcial-intelligence chips from going to China,” WSJ reported, and Nvidia’s reportedly $25 million donation to the White House ballroom.

“It is not just an intelligence issue; it’s also a potential corruption issue,” Blumenthal said. “There needs to be a really penetrating, comprehensive investigation of all the possible compromises of our intelligence that may have occurred, but also… that Donald Trump is so high on the head of Nvidia, and now is potentially linked to intelligence compromises.”

Trump has profited off Nvidia’s success while in office, buying “millions of dollars worth of Nvidia shares in his personal brokerage accounts since returning to oﬃce in 2025,” the WSJ reported. The White House maintains that the president has no role in managing his stock portfolio.

Other officials advising Trump on AI also benefited from relaxing export curbs, TOP said. On Tuesday, the group issued a report summarizing what the public knows about potential conflicts of interest of two Trump officials: former White House AI Czar David Sacks and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Haworth, TOP’s founder, told Ars she’s concerned that Sacks and Lutnick abused their power to convince Trump to let Nvidia sell cutting-edge technology to China, while standing to “gain astronomical amounts of money.”

“The public is outraged by Nvidia’s CEO for compromising our national security, but we didn’t get here because of Jensen Huang’s missteps alone,” Haworth said. If “Nvidia was knowingly doing business with companies tied to illegal chip sales and smuggling with China,” then “the Trump administration was asleep at the wheel,” she said.

items.content:
마이크로소프트(MS)가 오픈AI와 앤트로픽의 첨단 모델에 근접한 코딩 성능을 훨씬 낮은 비용으로 구현한 자체 AI 모델 'MAI 코드 2(MAI Code 2)'를 공개했다. 사이버 보안과 AI 에이전트의 판단 작업에 특화한 모델도 함께 선보이며, 외부 AI 모델에 대한 의존도를 줄이고 자체 모델 경쟁력을 강화하고 나섰다.

MS는 17일(현지시간) 미국 샌프란시스코에서 열린 연례 기술 행사 '이그나이트 2026'에서 코딩 전문 모델 'MAI 코드 2'와 경량형 'MAI 코드 2 플래시(MAI Code 2 Flash)', 보안 전문 모델 'MAI 사이버 2 플래시(MAI Cyber 2 Flash)'를 공개했다. AI 에이전트의 판단 작업에 특화한 '마이크로소프트 디시전 1.1(Microsoft-Decision-1.1)'도 정식 출시했다.

이번 발표의 핵심인 MAI 코드 2는 대규모 코드 저장소를 분석하고 여러 파일에 걸친 기능 수정과 오류 해결, 테스트 및 검증까지 수행하는 코딩 모델이다. 화면 캡처나 UI 시안을 바탕으로 웹사이트와 애플리케이션의 화면을 제작하는 작업도 지원한다.

MAI 코드 2는 총 2조8000억개 매개변수의 전문가 혼합(MoE) 모델로, 추론 과정에서는 800억개를 활성화한다. 최대 105만토큰의 컨텍스트와 이미지 입력을 지원하며, 약 50조토큰의 데이터로 사전학습한 뒤 깃허브 코파일럿의 실제 개발 환경에서 강화학습을 진행했다.

성능은 오픈AI와 앤트로픽의 상위 모델에 근접하는 수준이다. 4개 코딩 벤치마크의 평균 성능에서 MAI 코드 2는 'GPT-6.1 솔'의 98%를 기록하면서 비용은 40% 수준이었다. 앤트로픽의 '클로드 오퍼스 5.5'와 비교해서도 성능은 96%에 달했지만, 비용은 5%에 그쳤다.

UI와 게임, 데이터 시각화 등을 제작하는 블라인드 평가에서도 258명의 평가자가 참여한 가운데 MAI 코드 2가 생성한 결과물이 GPT-6 솔보다 낫다는 선택이 67%를 차지했다. 이들 수치는 MS의 자체 평가 결과이며, 비용 비교에는 50% 프로모션 가격이 적용됐다.

동시에 공개한 MAI 코드 2 플래시는 반복적인 개발 업무를 저렴하게 처리하는 경량 모델이다. 총 3980억개 매개변수 중 120억개를 활성화하며, 상위 모델과 동일한 105만토큰 컨텍스트를 지원한다. MS는 'GPT-6 루나'와 '클로드 하이쿠 5.5'에 근접한 코딩 성능을 각각 65%, 20%의 비용으로 제공한다고 설명했다.

기업 고객의 적용 사례도 공개했다. 미국 통신사 AT&T는 자체 업무에 맞게 조정한 플래시 모델이 5G 네트워크 분석에서 GPT-6.1 솔보다 높은 성능을 보이면서 비용은 50분의 1 수준이었다고 밝혔다. 도요타의 소프트웨어 개발 계열사 우븐 바이 도요타도 자동차 코딩 표준에 맞춰 모델을 미세조정한 결과, 기존 최첨단 모델보다 저렴하면서 실제 업무에 적용할 수 있는 코드 생성 능력이 개선됐다고 설명했다.

MAI 코드 2와 플래시는 깃허브 코파일럿에서 이용할 수 있으며, 플래시는 MS의 AI 개발 플랫폼인 마이크로소프트 파운드리에서도 제한적으로 제공된다.

사이버 보안 분야에서는 소프트웨어 취약점 탐지와 보안 사고 조사에 특화한 'MAI 사이버 2 플래시'를 공개했다.

취약점 탐지·재현 평가인 '사이버짐 E2E(CyberGym-E2E)'에서 92.3%의 성공률을 기록해 GPT-6 아스트라의 91.5%와 비슷한 성능을 보였으며, 작업당 비용은 2% 미만이었다.

MS는 다음 달 중순부터 일부 고객을 대상으로 자사 보안 에이전트 시스템에 통합할 예정이다.

AI 에이전트의 판단 작업에 특화한 '마이크로소프트 디시전 1.1'도 정식 출시했다. 요청에 맞는 도구 선택이나 작업 분류 등 간단한 판단을 빠르고 저렴하게 처리하는 모델로, 이번 버전에는 이미지 입력 기능이 추가됐다. 이미 4000곳 이상의 고객이 이 모델을 사용했다.

이번 발표는 MS가 오픈AI와 앤트로픽 등 외부 기업의 모델을 활용하는 동시에 자체 AI 모델 개발을 강화하고 있음을 보여준다. 특히 코딩처럼 사용량이 많은 분야에서 자체 모델이 경쟁력을 확보하면 외부 모델 사용 비용을 줄이고 코파일럿 등 AI 서비스의 수익성을 높일 수 있다.

무스타파 술레이만 MS AI CEO는 로이터와의 인터뷰에서 "이번 성과는 단일 모델에 그치지 않는다. 일시적인 성과도 아니다"라며 "우리는 성능과 가격을 동시에 최적화하며 지속적으로 개선하는 시스템을 구축했다"라고 말했다.

MS는 기업 고객에게 자체 AI 모델의 가중치를 라이선스 방식으로 제공하는 'MAI 라이선스드 웨이츠(MAI Licensed Weights)' 전략도 발표했다. 기업이 모델을 자체 업무에 맞게 조정하도록 지원하는 것으로, API 공급을 넘어 기업용 맞춤형 모델 시장까지 겨냥한 움직임이다.

MS는 이와 별도로 범용 최첨단 AI 모델도 개발하고 있다. 외부 모델과 자체 모델을 함께 공급하면서, 특정 업무에 최적화한 모델을 통해 비용 경쟁력과 기업 고객 확보를 동시에 추진한다는 전략이다.

items.title: Waymo Pauses All Highway Rides After California Safety Ban
items.summary: California’s DMV banned Waymo’s self-driving cars from freeways after determining that they pose “an imminent hazard to public safety.”
items.content:
Waymo self-driving taxis are no longer driving on highways after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its vehicles from state freeway operations. The ban, which the DMV says began on November 11, comes after the department determined that Waymo ’s freeway driving poses “an imminent hazard to public safety.”

In response, Waymo says it has stopped highway driving in all of its markets. The company may continue testing its vehicles on non-California highways with safety operators behind the wheels.

The ban follows two recent concerning incidents, California DMV spokesperson Jonathan Groveman wrote in a statement. In one, three Waymos entered an active highway construction closure on Route 101 on the San Francisco Peninsula. The other was captured in a viral video showing a Waymo vehicle interfering with California Highway Patrol cars on a San Francisco highway as they tried to enforce a “traffic break” as workers cleared debris from the crash.

Groveman said the California ban will remain in place until Waymo has proved that it has “taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies" that led to the incidents. It’s unclear how long that process will take.

In a written statement to WIRED, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher said the company is “working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo vehicles will continue to operate on surface streets in the 15 metros where it offers taxi service, including portions of Los Angeles, San Diego, and the San Francisco Bay Area.

This is the second time Waymo has publicly restricted its freeway operations after beginning to transport passengers on them last year . In June, the company recalled its software after federal regulators found that its system failed to recognize highway construction zones. Regulators with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) cited several incidents in April and May in which Waymo cars drove past ramp closure signs and into active lane closures. The events did not lead to collisions or injuries.

The NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last week, the agency said it was examining whether another Waymo recall software fix had actually solved its robotaxis’ safety issues. This recall, which occurred last December, was tied to incidents in which Waymo cars repeatedly drove by stopped school buses with their lights on and/or stop arms extended .

Self-driving cars have struggled with construction zones for at least a decade . The zones can look and be arranged differently based on what sort of construction is being done, and where. While humans can easily understand bollards, placards, and blinking arrows, the lack of hard-and-fast rules has proven difficult to reliably program into driving software. The issue is especially hazardous at high freeway speeds, where workers exist alongside fast-moving car traffic.

items.title: Model ML raises $250M to automate investment banking grunt work
items.summary: The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
items.content:
Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors.

Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022.

Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.

Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April.

Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results.

Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel.

In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris.

He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected.

In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today.

Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another.

Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia .

In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon.

"Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway.

He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics.

Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk .

Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side.

Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night.

In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow.

In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow.

Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern.

"Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance."

In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected.

He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier.

Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans .

Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence.

Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia .

"How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?"

"Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder.

Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second.

"So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says.

Was Rømer's finding quickly accepted by other scientists?

"It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder.

Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things.

"The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder.

Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains.

"Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder.

This became very important for astronomy.

"Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says.

This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved.

items.title: Google expands access to Gemini Tasks, which can help with calls, purchases
items.summary: Gemini's Task mode can help users coordinate calls, log into websites, and even make purchases on the user's behalf.
items.content:
Google is expanding the rollout of Tasks, a toggle in Gemini that converts the chatbot into a more active helper.

Unlike Gemini’s Chat, which merely allows users to talk to Google’s AI assistant for informational purposes, Tasks empowers the app to complete basic secretarial functions, deputizing it as a kind of personal assistant.

How, specifically, can you use it? Google says that the app can call businesses and book appointments on users’ behalf; it can also complete purchases for them via Google Pay, and even sign into websites securely if prompted to do so.

In a blog post , Josh Woodword, VP of Gemini, claims to have recently used the feature to call local car dealerships to schedule a service appointment for his family’s minivan. He says he also used it to analyze his electrical bill.

Getting the function up and running is easy. Users merely flip a toggle within the app from Chat to Tasks, which enables the feature. Users can also send texts to Gemini or call the app to give it commands.

items.title: Solid 2.0
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.solidjs.com/blog/solid-2-0-the-long-hold/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50536387 Points: 237 # Comments: 61
items.content:
5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then.

A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler.

More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time.

Today that solution reaches stable.

If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design.

This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands:

This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth.

SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below.

This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability.

"But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in.

Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong.

In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix:

These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime.

This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds.

We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX , both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring.

I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive.

Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another.

We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability.

And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use.

items.title: Phrack 73 Released
items.summary: Article URL: https://phrack.org/issues/73/introduction_md Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535992 Points: 291 # Comments: 45
items.content:
Last year marked the 40th anniversary of Phrack so we went big. We published our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some additional variations at several conferences around the world including AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon, OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone.

More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart.

We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners, donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We appreciate everyone who did it.

And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile. That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this issue is the follow-through.

This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and culture that grew around this work.

We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous underwater vehicles. There is also work examining backdoors in machine learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for continuing to put challenges in a zine.

We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to reverse engineering and security research are legendary.

In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities.

We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued even higher.

We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are excited to be a part of it.

Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue to put together, and some of you should be in it!

To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore vitality to Phrack, we thank you.

Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU], Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon

Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield, TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX, Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar, Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with smaller donations.

Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser, h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many others who submitted their work for consideration.

Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern, jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck

All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack.

The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next generation.

All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability of the editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible, all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are not omniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possible something contained within this publication is incorrect in some way. If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correct it in a future issue.

items.title: Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.
items.summary: In the Codename MDASH pilot, GitHub and Microsoft turned thousands of raw AI findings into 99 checked, private reports with suggested fixes for six widely used open source projects. Maintainers have already fixed more than half. The post Maintainers don’t need more AI bug reports
items.content:
AI has made finding potential vulnerabilities fast and cheap. Fixing them still takes human judgment, and in open source, that work falls to maintainers. Many are already flooded with AI-generated security findings, including duplicates and reports that aren’t vulnerabilities at all. Another raw scan doesn’t help them. Anyone pointing a new model at a project should ask its maintainers first and come with fixes, not just findings.

Maintainers are under intense pressure from this flood of reports. As Christian Grobmeier, a maintainer of Log4j, has put it, the AI defending open source has to be better than the AI attacking it .

AI shouldn’t add to maintainers’ workload. So, with maintainers, GitHub and Microsoft ran a pilot together: could AI help maintainers ship fixes instead of handing them more findings?

GitHub and Microsoft are using Codename MDASH , Microsoft’s multi-model agentic scanning harness, to find and fix security vulnerabilities in widely used open source software, strengthening the foundation that much of the world’s code is built on.

Our pilot had two goals: send only findings that matter, and never send a maintainer an unverified finding. Here’s how it worked:

Reports and fixes stayed on GitHub, where maintainers already work.

The result: Codename MDASH, using Microsoft’s MAI Cyber model, flagged thousands of possible issues across the six projects. After AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports. As of November 15, they had fixed 55, and 14 of those fixes were already in a release.

These lessons come from what the six projects fixed and what their maintainers chose to share. Six projects is a small sample, so read them as early lessons.

Fixing is where maintainers spend their time. So every report arrived already checked, with a suggested fix to review, adapt, and merge. Maintainers started from a well-scoped patch, not a raw finding.

The first fixes shipped about a week after the initial scan. Caddy’s maintainers fixed all 22 of the reports they received in a week or less. Maintainers used the suggested fixes, some as written and some with changes.

AutoGPT’s maintainers had recently shipped a new check, and it was broken. The report landed three days later and pointed at the right line. They took the fix further than the suggested patch, wrote it within a day, and had it in production less than a week later.

Finding vulnerabilities is no longer our bottleneck. Fixing them is the hard part, and that depends on maintainers.

Maintainers got a short list, not a flood. Express maintainers said the reports cut through the noise. Caddy maintainers said they surfaced obscure bugs and filled gaps that earlier reports had missed. For FastMCP, the scan went beyond what AI scanners had given them before. ImageMagick, maintained by a two-person team, received 22 reports.

AI did the finding, researchers did the checking, and maintainers stayed in charge.

One ImageMagick report looked like a kind of issue the maintainers had seen before. Its summary showed it wasn’t and pointed to the exact lines of code. They were able to push a fix in 15 minutes.

Normally, a security advisory would take us around 30 minutes to 1 hour on average to read, understand, and make a fix. It is a huge difference.

Codename MDASH was able to find unknown, obscure security bugs in our project with succinct reports, and it filled in gaps from some prior reports that hadn’t been noticed.

The pilot worked because people did careful work at every step, and that work doesn’t scale yet. Seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings by hand. Meanwhile, low-quality reports still reach maintainers every day.

For open source, fixes need to be delivered via private vulnerability reporting (PVR). Maintainers need to run CI/CD tests on private forks to verify those fixes. And to close the gap between defenders and attackers, maintainers need access to cyber-capable models to verify a proof of concept, before and after the fix.

The Codename MDASH scan provided unique insights into the security of our project above and beyond what AI scanners have provided us in the past

If you’re a maintainer, this approach changes what a security report costs you. A checked, private report that comes with a suggested fix takes less of your time. You shouldn’t have to triage a scanner’s output. That’s the sender’s job.

If you use AI to find vulnerabilities in open source, maintainers’ feedback points to this standard:

Features are easier and easier to ship, but in the future maintaining software will probably come down to who cares enough to manage the security.

Codename MDASH is very useful for cutting through the noise of vulnerability reports.

Everyone downstream benefits from this system. When a maintainer publishes a security advisory on GitHub and it’s reviewed for the GitHub Advisory Database, Dependabot can alert the repositories that depend on that package. That’s the idea behind the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund: 216 projects so far, with more than 300 maintainers fixing more than 4,000 vulnerabilities in software downloaded more than 20 billion times a month.

To the maintainers of AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, and Netty: thank you for your time, your trust, and your feedback. Thank you also to the Codename MDASH team at Microsoft Security, the MAI Cyber team, the researchers of Microsoft FORGE Lab, and GitHub Security Lab.

Maintainers do the fixing. Our job is to make sure they never do it alone.

Hear from maintainers about their experience with Codename MDASH. 👇

All six projects in this pilot are alumni of the GitHub Secure Open Source Fund , which gives each project $10,000 through GitHub Sponsors, plus security training and a supportive alumni community.

items.title: MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash
items.summary: Article URL: https://microsoft.ai/news/introducing-mai-code-2-and-mai-code-2-flash/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50535885 Points: 295 # Comments: 136
items.content:
MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash : t wo new coding models built for the everyday enterprise coding tasks , delivering leading performance at a fraction of the cost of competing models.

MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost.

Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost.

To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work.

Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost. 1

MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. 2

In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 6 5% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks. 3

MAI Code 2 is also becoming the workhorse behind Microsoft products. From Code 2 Flash we further optimized a single model, MAI Work Flash, to serve multiple Microsoft products across M365 and Fabric IQ.

Excel: Our model is on par for accuracy and token efficiency with GPT 6 Luna across key internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks.

PowerPoint: On key production benchmark scenarios that measure frequent PowerPoint tasks, our model performs on par with GPT 6 Luna in both quality and token efficiency.

Word: Our model performs similar to GPT 6.1 sol (while being significantly smaller) on 5 key internal benchmarks using ~42% fewer input tokens per call than GPT6.1 Sol in production.

Teams: Our model beats GPT 6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling knowledge gaps, and adapting custom instructions using up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling.

FabricIQ: In offline evaluation runs our MAI model outperforms GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6-astra, and Opus-5.5 at DAX query generation, the core capability behind “Chat with your Data” for Power BI semantic models.

MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, and Code 2 Flash is in limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . Soon, we’ll be releasing it on Open Router, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo.

Learn more about customizing MAI Code 2 on our Custom Models page.

items.title: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices
items.summary: Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud. The post Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.

In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.

GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.

At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity.

Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.

The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.

At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior . Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol , the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.

You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.

The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.

Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.

Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The Copilot Chat extension, which used to provide all of VS Code’s AI and agentic capabilities, had been growing for over three years, reaching over 400,000 lines of TypeScript, not counting tests. But, as a VS Code extension, it was structured around the lifecycle of a VS Code window and depended entirely on the VS Code extension API. Neither that lifetime nor those APIs would be available in a standalone agent host process.

As we started building the Agent Host Protocol in early 2026, the Copilot SDK was also being developed, and it made sense to leverage it as the foundation for the new agentic stack. This was a big transition. It’s easy to build a harness implementation that says hello and can edit files—we were using the agent host to develop the agent host after the first couple weeks—but it’s another thing to build one that covers the long tail of features developers had come to expect from Copilot Chat.

GitHub has had Copilot cloud agents for a couple of years, allowing developers to run tasks in the cloud from any device. While VS Code was quietly developing the Agent Host Protocol, GitHub was looking to expand that capability to coordinate sessions running on your own devices via the Copilot app, or in cloud sandboxes. This was exactly the N:M problem that AHP was built to solve, so adopting the same technology made perfect sense.

From the outset, the GitHub Agent Host had different requirements than VS Code’s implementation. VS Code runs the host locally and can drop its host on other compute over SSH, containers, WSL, or Dev Tunnels, and it is actually included as part of the VS Code Server bundle. The GitHub Agent Host needed to run in the cloud and across a much wider variety of infrastructure, environments, and security constraints.

items.title: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
items.summary: AG: OpenAI tested dangerous AI without proper oversight and misled public about it.
items.content:
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.

The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”

OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release .

OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.

In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.

Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”

The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents. Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.

“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit filed yesterday said.

OpenAI told Ars that most of the incidents identified in its review had low severity, and none matched the severity or scale of the Hugging Face attack. OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.

“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI said. “We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment. This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the attorney general’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”

California’s lawsuit accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance as defined in state law, and several violations of the state’s Unfair Competition Law. Alleged violations include “causing and/or allowing agents to gain unauthorized access to third-party computer systems,” developing AI models without adequate security measures, and making false or misleading claims about the safety of its AI products.

California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages. It also wants an order to “compel OpenAI to abate the ongoing public nuisance their conduct has created in California.” Bonta said in his press release that “the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability—and this was only one of 80 known incidents.”

OpenAI was sued in September by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), a nonprofit that alleged violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and the state’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said. “Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”

OpenAI said in response to the LASST lawsuit that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.”

items.title: The Nvidia Scandal Could Upend Chip Sales to China. Trump Wants to Keep Them Going
items.summary: Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick has been under attack for not blacklisting a company caught up in the Jensen Huang scandal. But Trump is on board with the policy.
items.content:
After days of political fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang ’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, President Donald Trump is defending commerce secretary Howard Lutnick.

Last week, Lutnick came under fire from treasury secretary Scott Bessent for not aggressively imposing export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

But Trump’s defense of Lutnick, sources tell WIRED, reflects the president's own view that allowing the sale of some advanced AI chips to China can keep China reliant on US technology and simultaneously boost US tech stocks.

Lutnick “was doing that because if you didn’t delay it, if you didn’t do something, you could have a blowup with China. We’re having a very good relationship with China right now,” Trump said ahead of a multiday trip to Asia and a meeting on Thursday with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Trump convened an Oval Office meeting on November 5 to discuss the political fallout from Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive whom some in the US government believe was recruited to spy for China, according to two sources briefed on the discussion.

Megaspeed received advanced AI chips manufactured by Nvidia through several layers of companies that started with a subsidiary of a blacklisted Chinese server conglomerate called Inspur, The New York Times has reported .

In the meeting, the sources say, Bessent confronted Lutnick, asking why Megaspeed was not added to the entity list faster, given that secretary of state Marco Rubio and US trade representative Jamieson Greer, among others, had already agreed it was the correct move.

Lutnick responded that he would defer to Trump and would add Megaspeed to the entity list if that was what the president wanted, the sources say.

But Trump settled on a third approach: for Lutnick to work on introducing a new interim trade rule to stop Chinese AI labs from using advanced AI chips remotely by leasing their compute power from data centers in Southeast Asia.

In a statement to WIRED, a White House spokesperson said the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.” (Superintelligence, or SI, is the administration’s term for artificial intelligence.)

A senior White House official added that Trump has been adamant that Chinese firms cannot acquire the most advanced Nvidia chips, known as Blackwells and Rubins. Those are different from the H200-type chips, built on previous-generation Hopper architecture, that Megaspeed was acquiring.

Lutnick’s position appears to have been based on a series of considerations, the sources say. For one, Megaspeed has already had the chips for months, and blacklisting the company would be akin to playing whack-a-mole unless the administration dealt with the underlying issue of Chinese firms getting remote access to US chips.

Meanwhile, Lutnick has moved cautiously on any new export restrictions—essentially waiting to get explicit approval from Trump—after he faced heavy criticism in 2025 for expanding restrictions against firms with Chinese ties, the sources said.

In September 2025, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security started aggressively using the so-called affiliates rule , which automatically extends trade restrictions to any company that is 50 percent owned by a company already on the US entity list or the military end-user list.

But the move prompted immediate retaliation by China, which suspended exports of critical rare earth metals to the US and, the sources said, prompted a wave of internal criticism accusing the Commerce Department of having sparked a trade war.

After the Busan summit at the end of October 2025, where Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping agreed to a trade truce, the White House instructed Commerce to halt the use of the affiliates rule and clear new export controls in advance, the sources said.

The suspension of the affiliates rule—which came almost as soon as it was implemented—may have had a knock-on effect on companies like Megaspeed, one person familiar with deliberations said.

Inspur, the Chinese server conglomerate connected to Megaspeed, operated a subsidiary called Aivres, which, as a California-based company, could legally buy restricted Nvidia chips without triggering direct export bans and ship them internationally to Southeast Asia.

In total, Aivres transferred billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips, including the powerful H200 chips, to Megaspeed’s subsidiaries.

Instead of shipping the physical chips into China, Megaspeed hosted servers at data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia—then rented out compute power to major Chinese companies. A spokesperson for Aivres said in a statement that the company complies with all US export controls.

items.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
items.summary: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water
items.content:
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River . And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study . Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
